title: Bank Liability for Scam Transfers: A Consumer Commission View
description: A recent Consumer Commission ruling held a bank liable even when a customer voluntarily transferred funds to a scammer. The commission found the bank negligen.

faq.q: Does an OTP always mean I'm liable for a scam transaction?
faq.a: Not necessarily. While an OTP signifies authorisation, recent consumer commission rulings suggest banks can still be held liable if they fail to detect and act on suspicious transaction patterns, even with OTP-authorised transfers.

faq.q: What if I report the scam late?
faq.a: Prompt reporting is crucial. Delay in reporting can reduce your chances of recovering funds, as it gives fraudsters more time to move the money. However, even if reported late, a bank's negligence in monitoring transactions can still be a basis for a claim.

faq.q: What are my rights under RBI guidelines for fraud?
faq.a: The RBI's circular on "Customer Protection – Limiting Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions" outlines scenarios where customer liability is zero, limited, or full, primarily for *unauthorised* transactions. While "authorised but fraudulent" transactions are a grey area, the spirit of protection remains.

faq.q: Can I appeal a bank's decision if they deny my fraud claim?
faq.a: Yes, if your bank denies your claim, you can escalate the matter to the Banking Ombudsman (if it's an RBI-regulated entity) or file a complaint with the Consumer Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

faq.q: What is the bank's responsibility in preventing scams?
faq.a: Banks are expected to have robust fraud detection systems, monitor for suspicious transaction patterns, and take proactive steps to protect customers, such as verifying unusual transactions. Failure to do so can be considered a deficiency in service.
